newsitem.title: ITALY: CYCLING-GIRO WINNER GOTTI TARGETS TOUR DE FRANCE.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-GIRO WINNER GOTTI TARGETS TOUR DE FRANCE.

text.p: Ivan Gotti became the first home winner of the Giro d'Italia for six years on Sunday.
After a succession of Spanish, Swiss and Russian victories, the slim Italian headed Russian rival and defending champion Pavel Tonkov by one minute 27 seconds on the final run tino Milan.
Franco Chioccioli, the last Italian to win a Giro in 1991, said: "I don't think we will have to wait another six years for the next. Now we have Gotti, Marco Pantani, and Francesco Casagrande."
Gotti has next month's Tour de France as his next target. "It will be a powerful line-up, but I believe that our team and myself can find our place among those big names," he said.
"This day, however, has been full of emotion for me. The first time I believed that I could keep the leader's pink jersey came after the time trial four days ago."
Gotti's team mate Mario Cipollini crowned the day with his fifth stage win as he beat off Sweden's Glenn Magnusson and Italian Luca Mazzanti in the closing 165 km leg from Boario Terme.
It was his 21st Giro stage win and lifted the big Tuscan into the 10 most successful stage-winners, but still only halfway to the record 42 of Alfredo Binda.
Cipollini spent the first two days in the leader's pink jersey until Tonkov took over for 11 days. The Italian also held the jersey for top points scorer throughout the 22-day, 3,918 km race.
"We have achieved more as a team than we predicted. It is one of the best moments of my life," said Cipollini who became a father last week.

"Gotti has given a lot to Italy, and I am sure that it will not be the only success. He has 'grown' a lot since I first knew him, and I am sure that he will be ready for the yellow jersey in the Tour."
Crashes, illness and injury took their toll, eliminating major hopes Pantani, Frenchman Luc Leblanc, Italian Enrico Zaina, and Russian Piotr Ugrumov.

The casualty list of 70 has been surpassed only three times in the last 40 years. "The Giro is so important that everyone takes too many risks, and they crash," said Magnusson after finishing second on Milan's Parco Sempione circuit.
